v: Right now, beneath Calgary's streets, nearly thirty-three thousand sewer pipes have passed the life that pipes like them are expected to last.
And if none were replaced, that number would more than double by twenty seventy-one. So, how old are the pipes under your feet?
The City of Calgary publishes every public sewer connection. Nearly three hundred sixty-eight thousand of them, about two thousand eight hundred kilometres of pipe.
Each record has the year the pipe went in, and what it's made of. We set each pipe's age against published service lives for its material: a short, a typical, and a long benchmark.
The typical connection went in in nineteen ninety-five, so it's thirty-one years old. But one in four is more than fifty.

Two in three are plastic, built to last a century or more. One in five is clay tile, mostly from the sixties and seventies. Cast iron, with the shortest life, is three percent. And half of it is already past its typical life.
Against the typical life for each material, about nine percent of connections are past it. Judged by the short end of the range, it's one in four. By the long end, about two percent.

One honest caveat. Four in five of the pipes past their typical life have no material on record, so the study gives them a cautious forty-five years. Age is a warning sign, not proof that a pipe has failed.

The oldest networks are in the inner city. In Inglewood, Renfrew and Banff Trail, the typical connection dates from the mid nineteen-fifties. In Wildwood, three in four connections are past their typical life.
In the newest communities, like Alpine Park and Glacier Ridge, the typical pipe is just two or three years old.

The bigger story is the wave behind them. The boom years of the seventies laid more connections than any decade before. As those pipes age, the count past typical life climbs. About forty-three thousand by twenty forty-six, and seventy-eight thousand by twenty seventy-one.

The City is already fixing pipes from the inside, sliding a new liner through the old one, without digging up the street. Relining has more than tripled, from about two hundred fifty connections in twenty seventeen, to seven hundred ninety-one in twenty twenty-five.
Residents feel it too. In twenty twenty-five, Calgarians made about fourteen thousand three-one-one requests about sewer back-ups, sewer maintenance and catch basins.

Calgary isn't alone. Across Canada, thirteen percent of smaller sewer pipes were rated poor or very poor in twenty twenty-two. And the City's own risk report lists nine large wastewater river crossings, of unknown condition, as a severe risk.
What the open data can't show is condition. The City doesn't publish its sewer mains, or its pipe inspections. With those, age could become a true picture of risk.
